title: The Valedictory I Never Gave
script: Narrator: [wistful] They asked me to say a few words at my own retirement dinner, and I declined, ostensibly out of modesty, though the truer reason was that thirty-one years resist compression into anything a room full of colleagues could politely applaud between courses.
Narrator: [wry] So here, instead, is the valedictory I withheld, addressed to no audience but the ceiling of my study and whatever remains of my vanity.

Narrator: [reflective] I did not become a better teacher by accumulating certainty, as the brochures would have you believe; I became one by relinquishing it, semester by grudging semester, until I could stand before a lecture hall and confess ignorance without flinching.

Narrator: [candid] The students who unsettled me most were never the indifferent ones but the earnest ones, the sort who took my offhand remarks as doctrine and quoted them back to me years later with a reverence I hadn't earned and privately found alarming.

Narrator: [thoughtful] I used to believe my discipline was in decline, that each incoming cohort read less carefully than the last, and I have since concluded this was less an observation than an occupational vanity, the comforting delusion that one's own generation marked some high-water mark of seriousness.
Narrator: [wry] Every generation of professors, I suspect, mistakes its own fading stamina for the world's decline.

Narrator: [with feeling] What I will actually miss is unglamorous: the particular hush before a seminar turns, the moment a mediocre argument suddenly reorganizes itself into something rigorous under gentle interrogation.

Narrator: [honest] I never once cured a student of laziness through eloquence alone; the ones who changed did so quietly, on their own schedule, usually for reasons that had nothing to do with anything I'd said.
Narrator: [gently] Vanity again, perhaps, but I'd like to think I occasionally supplied the pretext under which that private transformation felt permissible.

Narrator: [resolved] So, no valedictory, no applause between courses. Only this: teaching was never the noble transmission of certainty I'd imagined at twenty-five. It was the slower, humbler art of admitting what I did not know, convincingly enough that someone else felt safe admitting it too.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator decline to give a speech at her retirement dinner?
options: Thirty-one years resisted compression into something suitable for polite applause between courses
She was too emotional to speak
The event organizers forgot to invite her
quiz.explanation: She says the truer reason was that thirty-one years resist compression into anything a room could politely applaud between courses.

quiz.question: According to the narrator, how did she become a better teacher?
options: By relinquishing certainty, semester by grudging semester
quiz.explanation: She says she became a better teacher by relinquishing certainty, not accumulating it.

quiz.question: Which students unsettled the narrator most?
options: The earnest ones who quoted her offhand remarks back as doctrine
quiz.explanation: She says the earnest students who treated her remarks as doctrine unsettled her most.

quiz.question: What conclusion does she reach about believing her discipline was in decline?
options: It was likely an occupational vanity, mistaking her own fading stamina for the world's decline
It only applied to certain students
quiz.explanation: She concludes every generation of professors mistakes its own fading stamina for the world's decline.

quiz.question: What does the narrator conclude teaching actually was?
options: The humbler art of admitting what she did not know, convincingly enough for others to do the same
quiz.explanation: She concludes teaching was the humbler art of admitting ignorance convincingly enough that students felt safe doing the same.
